title: Measurements and Experimentation
tagline: SI units, Vernier callipers, screw gauge and the simple pendulum

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Physics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every numerical result in this chapter was independently recomputed by scripts/verify-math.mjs. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Every physical quantity is useless without a number and a unit attached to it, and a number is meaningless unless you know how precisely it was measured. This chapter deals with both halves of that problem. On one side are the SI units and the instrument known as the metre rule, together with Vernier callipers and the screw gauge for measuring very small lengths. On the other side is the simple pendulum, the classic Class 9 experiment, which turns a stopwatch and a piece of string into a measurement of the gravitational field of the Earth. The accuracy of an instrument and the precision of a reading are different ideas, and confusing them is the most common exam error in this unit.

learn.title: Physical quantities, SI units and the metre rule

blocks.text: A physical quantity is anything that can be measured, such as length, mass, time or force. Measuring it means comparing it with a standard of the same kind, and that standard is the unit. The International System of Units, or SI, fixes seven base units from which nearly all other units are built.

items.meaning: One of the seven independent units: metre for length, kilogram for mass, second for time, ampere for current, kelvin for temperature, mole for amount of substance, candela for luminous intensity.
A unit built from base units, such as the newton, which is one kilogram metre per second squared.
The smallest quantity an instrument can measure, equal to the value of one smallest division. It fixes the accuracy of the instrument.

items: The metre rule is 100 cm long, and its least count is 0.1 cm, that is 1 mm.
1 hour = 60 minutes, 1 minute = 60 seconds, so 1 hour = 3600 seconds.
Length is measured in metre, mass in kilogram and time in second in SI.

items.text: A rod is measured as 45.0 cm with a metre rule of least count 0.1 cm. What is the greatest possible error?
items.note: The error is half the least count, that is 0.05 cm. The true length is therefore between 44.95 cm and 45.05 cm.

learn.title: Vernier callipers and the screw gauge

blocks.text: Both instruments work by comparing a main scale with a second scale whose divisions are deliberately made slightly different. When the two scales line up, the reading on the second scale tells you the fractional part that the main scale cannot resolve. The screw gauge does the same thing with a thread, and it can measure very small lengths because one complete turn of the screw advances the spindle by a known pitch.

items.meaning: A sliding secondary scale with n divisions, chosen so that n Vernier divisions equal n minus 1 main scale divisions.
Vernier scale division. In the standard form, 1 VSD = 10/n main scale divisions, where n is the number of Vernier divisions.
The distance moved by the screw in one complete turn, normally 0.5 mm or 1 mm.
The graduated drum of a screw gauge. Its least count is the pitch divided by the number of divisions on the drum, commonly 0.01 mm.

items: Vernier reading = main scale reading + coinciding division x value of one VSD, plus the zero error.
For a 10-division Vernier, 1 VSD = 0.9 main scale divisions = 0.09 cm, and the least count is 0.01 cm.
For a 20-division Vernier, 1 VSD = 0.95 main scale divisions = 0.095 cm, and the least count is 0.005 cm.
A screw gauge with pitch 0.5 mm and 50 circular divisions has least count 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm.
Always state whether the zero error is positive or negative, and add it with the correct sign.

items.text: A Vernier callipers has a main scale in cm and 10 Vernier divisions. The main scale reading is 3.4 cm and the 6th Vernier division coincides. What is the reading?
items.note: 1 VSD = 0.09 cm, so the reading is 3.4 + 6 x 0.09 = 3.4 + 0.54 = 3.94 cm.

items.text: A screw gauge has a pitch of 1 mm and 100 circular divisions. What is its least count?
items.note: Least count = pitch divided by the number of circular divisions = 1/100 = 0.01 mm.

learn.title: The simple pendulum and T = 2 pi root(l/g)

blocks.text: The simple pendulum is the standard experiment of this unit. A small metal ball, called the bob, hangs from a fixed point on an inextensible string. The bob is displaced slightly to one side and released, and the time for a fixed number of complete oscillations is measured with a stopwatch. The time period is the time for one complete oscillation, that is the time to return to the starting position and direction.

items.meaning: The time taken by the bob to complete one full oscillation. It is denoted by T.
One complete back-and-forth motion of the bob. Twenty complete oscillations are normally timed in the laboratory.

items: For small oscillations, T = 2 pi root(l/g), where l is the length of the string from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob and g is the acceleration due to gravity.
T is directly proportional to the square root of the length, so quadrupling the length doubles the time period.
T does not depend on the mass of the bob, so a heavy and a light bob of the same length give the same time period.
The string must be inextensible and the bob must be small, so that the effective length is well defined.
T is independent of the amplitude only for small oscillations, that is for angles of about 10 degrees or less.

items.text: Find the time period of a simple pendulum of length 0.99 m, taking g as 9.8 m per second squared.
items.note: T = 2 pi root(0.99/9.8) = 2 pi root(0.10102) = 2 pi x 0.31784 = 1.997 seconds, approximately 2.0 seconds.

items.text: If the length of a pendulum is made four times, by what factor does the time period change?
items.note: Since T is proportional to root(l), the factor is root 4 = 2, so the time period doubles.

learn.title: Accuracy, precision and the errors of measurement

blocks.text: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings to one another. A faulty metre rule can give readings that are always exactly the same to the last decimal place, so those readings are precise but not accurate. This distinction is the source of most conceptual questions on measurement.

items: Maximum error in a single reading = half the least count of the instrument.
Systematic error is a constant error, such as a zero error, that shifts every reading in the same direction.
Random error varies in size and sign from reading to reading, and is reduced by taking the mean of several readings.
Measuring the diameter of a sphere with a Vernier callipers is a standard Class 9 practical.

items.text: Three readings of a length are 5.2 cm, 5.3 cm and 5.3 cm. What is the mean, and what is the range?
items.note: The mean is (5.2 + 5.3 + 5.3)/3 = 15.8/3 = 5.2667 cm, approximately 5.27 cm. The range is 5.3 minus 5.2 = 0.1 cm.

keyPoints: SI base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature).
Least count is the smallest division an instrument can resolve, and it fixes its accuracy.
The metre rule has a least count of 0.1 cm; error in one reading is half of that, 0.05 cm.
In a Vernier callipers, n Vernier divisions equal n minus 1 main scale divisions.
For a 10-division Vernier the least count is 0.01 cm and 1 VSD = 0.09 cm.
Screw gauge least count = pitch divided by the number of circular divisions.
Time period of a simple pendulum, T = 2 pi root(l/g).
T is proportional to root(l) and is independent of the mass of the bob.
Accuracy is closeness to truth; precision is agreement between repeated readings.
Maximum error of one reading = half the least count.
Random error is reduced by averaging; systematic error is not.
examFocus: Vernier questions almost always require the coincidence multiplied by the value of one Vernier division, and students lose marks by using the main scale value of one division instead.
For the screw gauge, state the pitch and the number of circular divisions before dividing, and give the answer in millimetres.
Pendulum questions usually supply T and l and ask for g, or ask how T changes when l changes; the square-root relationship is the whole point.
Measuring the diameter of a sphere or a cylinder with Vernier callipers is a frequently set practical; include a precaution about tightening the screw gently so the ball is not flattened.

vocabulary.meaning: The smallest quantity an instrument can measure, set by its smallest division.
A sliding secondary scale whose divisions are made slightly smaller than the main scale divisions.
The distance the screw advances in one complete turn, used with the circular scale to find the least count.
The time taken by a pendulum to complete one full oscillation.
One complete back-and-forth motion of the pendulum bob.
A constant error that shifts every reading in the same direction.

questions.prompt: The SI unit of mass is:
questions.answer: kilogram
questions.explanation: Mass is measured in kilograms, which is the SI base unit of mass. The gram is a smaller unit and the tonne is 1000 kilograms. The newton is the SI unit of force, not mass.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the gram, which is the common unit of mass but not the SI base unit.

questions.prompt: The least count of a metre rule graduated in millimetres is:
questions.answer: 0.1 cm
questions.explanation: A millimetre is 0.1 cm, so the smallest graduation on the rule is 0.1 cm and that is its least count.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 1 cm, which treats each centimetre mark as the smallest division rather than each millimetre line.

questions.prompt: A Vernier callipers has 10 Vernier divisions. The value of one Vernier scale division in cm is:
questions.explanation: Ten Vernier divisions equal 9 main scale divisions of 1 cm each, so one VSD is 9/10 = 0.9 main scale divisions, which is 0.9 x 0.1 = 0.09 cm.
questions.commonMistake: Dividing by 10 instead of 9, which gives 0.1 cm and destroys the whole purpose of a Vernier.

questions.prompt: A screw gauge has a pitch of 0.5 mm and 50 circular divisions. Its least count is:
questions.explanation: Least count = pitch divided by the number of circular divisions = 0.5/50 = 0.01 mm.
questions.commonMistake: Giving the pitch itself, 0.5 mm, which is the advance per turn and not the resolution.

questions.prompt: The length of a simple pendulum is increased four times. Its time period will:
questions.answer: double
questions.explanation: T is proportional to the square root of the length, so multiplying the length by 4 multiplies T by root 4 = 2.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming T is directly proportional to length, which would make it four times as large.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the smallest quantity that an instrument can measure is called its ________.
questions.answer: least count, which fixes the accuracy of that instrument
questions.explanation: The least count is the value of the smallest division on the scale and sets the limit on how finely the instrument can read.
questions.commonMistake: Answering precision, which describes agreement between readings rather than what the instrument can resolve.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the time period T of a simple pendulum of length l is given by T = ________.
questions.answer: 2 pi root(l/g), where g is the acceleration due to gravity
questions.explanation: The standard formula for small oscillations relates the time period to the square root of the length divided by g.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 2 pi root(g/l), which inverts the relationship and is the single most common slip in this unit.

questions.prompt: Express 3.2 km in metres and in millimetres.
questions.answer: In metres: 3.2 km = 3.2 x 1000 m = 3200 m. In millimetres: 3200 m = 3200 x 1000 mm = 3200000 mm.
questions.explanation: Each step down the length scale multiplies by 1000, so 1 km is 1000000 mm.
questions.commonMistake: Converting to millimetres by multiplying by 100 only, forgetting there are two factors of 1000 to cross.

questions.prompt: Find the maximum possible error in a single reading taken with a metre rule of least count 0.1 cm, and state the range of true values if the reading is 38.5 cm.
questions.answer: The maximum error is half the least count, which is 0.05 cm. The true length is therefore between 38.5 minus 0.05 and 38.5 plus 0.05 cm, that is between 38.45 cm and 38.55 cm.
questions.explanation: The error is at most half a division either side, because the true position of the mark cannot lie outside the smallest graduation.
questions.commonMistake: Using the full least count of 0.1 cm as the error instead of half of it.

questions.prompt: A Vernier callipers has a main scale in cm and 10 Vernier divisions. The main scale reading is 2.7 cm and the 4th Vernier division coincides with a main scale mark. Find the reading.
questions.answer: Ten Vernier divisions equal 9 main scale divisions, so 1 VSD = 0.9 main scale divisions = 0.9 x 0.1 cm = 0.09 cm. The reading is 2.7 + 4 x 0.09 = 2.7 + 0.36 = 3.06 cm.
questions.explanation: The coincidence index times the value of one Vernier division is the fractional part the main scale cannot show, and it is added to the last visible main scale mark.
questions.commonMistake: Multiplying by 0.1 cm instead of 0.09 cm, which uses the main scale division in place of the Vernier division.

questions.prompt: A screw gauge with pitch 1 mm and 100 circular divisions reads 2.5 mm on the main scale and 30 divisions on the circular scale. Find the reading and state whether the instrument can resolve this value.
questions.answer: The least count is 1/100 = 0.01 mm. The circular scale reading is 30 x 0.01 mm = 0.30 mm. The total reading is 2.5 + 0.30 = 2.80 mm. Since the answer is quoted to two decimal places, matching the least count of 0.01 mm, the instrument can resolve it correctly.
questions.explanation: The circular scale contribution is the coincidence count multiplied by the least count, and the reading is only meaningful if quoted to that same precision.
questions.commonMistake: Reporting 2.5 mm and ignoring the circular scale, or quoting the answer as 2.8 mm when the least count is 0.01 mm.

questions.prompt: A student measures the diameter of a metal sphere with Vernier callipers and repeats the measurement three times, obtaining 1.24 cm, 1.27 cm and 1.26 cm. Find the mean diameter, the range, and state one precaution.
questions.answer: The mean is (1.24 + 1.27 + 1.26)/3 = 3.77/3 = 1.2567 cm, approximately 1.257 cm. The range is 1.27 minus 1.24 = 0.03 cm. Precautions: the sphere must be placed centrally between the jaws and the screw tightened gently so that the ball is not flattened or deformed; the reading should be taken along the greatest diameter of the sphere and viewed with the eye directly above the coincidence point to avoid parallax error.
questions.explanation: Averaging reduces random error, and the diameter should be measured at the greatest width of the sphere so the result is genuinely the diameter.
questions.commonMistake: Measuring along a smaller chord of the sphere instead of its greatest diameter, giving a value that is too small.

questions.prompt: Find the time period of a simple pendulum of length 1 m, taking pi as 22/7 and g as 9.8 m per second squared. Hence find the length of a pendulum that oscillates twice in every 3 seconds.
questions.answer: For the first part, T = 2 pi root(l/g) = 2 x (22/7) x root(1/9.8) = (44/7) x root(0.10204) = (44/7) x 0.31944 = 2.008 seconds, approximately 2.01 seconds. For the second part, the time period is 3/2 = 1.5 seconds. Using T = 2 pi root(l/g), l = g x (T/2pi)^2 = 9.8 x (1.5/(44/7))^2 = 9.8 x (1.5 x 7/44)^2 = 9.8 x (10.5/44)^2 = 9.8 x (0.23864)^2 = 9.8 x 0.056949 = 0.5581 m, approximately 0.558 m. Since the second pendulum is shorter and its period is shorter, this is consistent.
questions.explanation: Rearranging the formula gives l = g(T/2pi)^2, which is the form needed when T and g are known and l is required.
questions.commonMistake: Using T in place of T/2 in the rearranged formula, or forgetting to square the ratio.

questions.prompt: Why is the length of a pendulum measured from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob rather than to the lowest point of the bob?
questions.answer: The bob has a finite size, so it is really a small sphere rather than a point. The restoring force acts on the centre of mass of the bob, and the string tension also acts along the line to that centre, so the effective length of the pendulum is the distance from the point of suspension to the centre of mass. Measuring to the lowest point would add the radius of the bob and give a length that is too large by that amount, which would make the computed time period too large.
questions.explanation: The physics is governed by the centre of mass, so the effective length is measured to the centre of mass and not to the surface of the bob.
questions.commonMistake: Measuring to the bottom of the bob, which overestimates the length and hence the time period.

questions.prompt: A vernier callipers shows a negative zero error of 0.02 cm. The main scale reading is 5.6 cm and the 8th Vernier division coincides. Find the corrected reading.
questions.answer: Ten Vernier divisions equal 9 main scale divisions, so 1 VSD = 0.09 cm. The uncorrected reading is 5.6 + 8 x 0.09 = 5.6 + 0.72 = 6.32 cm. A negative zero error means the instrument reads less than the true value, so the correction must be added to the observed reading. The corrected reading is 6.32 + 0.02 = 6.34 cm.
questions.explanation: A negative zero error means the zero of the scale sits below the true zero, so every reading is too small and the error must be added back.
questions.commonMistake: Subtracting the negative zero error instead of adding it, which doubles the mistake rather than correcting it.

questions.prompt: State the difference between accuracy and precision, and give one situation in which readings are precise but not accurate.
questions.answer: Accuracy is how close a measured value is to the true value; precision is how close repeated measurements are to one another. A metre rule with a worn or damaged scale can give readings that agree to the last decimal place every time, so they are highly precise, yet if the scale is uniformly stretched every one of them is wrong by the same amount, so they are not accurate.
questions.explanation: Precision is about agreement between readings while accuracy is about agreement with truth, and a constant scale error produces precision without accuracy.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that a very precise instrument is automatically accurate, which is exactly what a systematic error prevents.

questions.prompt: A student times 20 oscillations of a pendulum and obtains 39.6 seconds. Find the time period and state how many oscillations should be counted to reduce the error.
questions.answer: The time period is the total time divided by the number of oscillations, so T = 39.6/20 = 1.98 seconds. Counting 20 oscillations rather than one reduces the relative error, because the stopwatch reaction-time error of about 0.2 to 0.3 seconds is then divided among 20 oscillations instead of one, making it 20 times smaller.
questions.explanation: Timing many oscillations and dividing by the count averages out the stopwatch error, which is why 20 is the standard number.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 39.6 seconds as the time period, which is the time for 20 oscillations and not for one.

questions.prompt: Two pendulums of the same length are made of different masses, one of iron and one of aluminium. Compare their time periods and explain.
questions.answer: Their time periods are equal, because T = 2 pi root(l/g) contains no term for the mass of the bob. The restoring force for a given angular displacement is proportional to the mass, since it is the component of the weight mg sin(theta) along the arc, and the inertia of the bob, which resists acceleration, is also proportional to its mass. The mass cancels, so the time period depends only on the effective length and on g.
questions.explanation: Both the restoring force and the inertia scale with mass, so the ratio between them, and hence the period, is independent of mass.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming the heavier bob swings more slowly because it has more inertia, forgetting that its restoring force is proportionally greater too.

questions.prompt: How many oscillations does a pendulum of time period 1.5 seconds complete in 45 seconds?
questions.answer: The number of oscillations is the total time divided by the time period, so 45/1.5 = 30 oscillations.
questions.explanation: Since T is the time for one complete oscillation, dividing the total time by T gives the number of complete oscillations.
questions.commonMistake: Dividing by 2T because an oscillation is a there-and-back motion, whereas one complete oscillation already includes both halves.

questions.prompt: State the SI units of length, mass, time and force, and state how the newton is defined in terms of base units.
questions.answer: Length is measured in metre, mass in kilogram and time in second, these being SI base units. Force is measured in newton. One newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kilogram an acceleration of 1 metre per second squared, so 1 N = 1 kg x 1 m per second squared = 1 kg m per second squared.
questions.explanation: The newton is a derived unit, obtained from mass and length and time through the definition F = ma.
questions.commonMistake: Giving the newton as a base unit rather than identifying kilogram, metre and second as the base units.

questions.prompt: Explain why a screw gauge can measure a hair's thickness while a metre rule cannot.
questions.answer: A metre rule has a least count of 0.1 cm, that is 1 mm, so it cannot resolve anything smaller than a millimetre. A hair is roughly 0.05 mm thick, which is far below a millimetre and would register as zero on a metre rule. A screw gauge has a least count of about 0.01 mm, so it can resolve the hair as a visible fraction of a millimetre. The finer resolution comes from the thread, which converts a very small rotational movement into a very small linear advance that the circular scale can count.
questions.explanation: The thread is what converts rotation into a fine linear displacement, giving a least count far smaller than any printed scale.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking the screw gauge works by making the jaws closer together by a large amount per turn, when in fact one turn gives only 0.5 or 1 mm of travel.

questions.prompt: A screw gauge has a pitch of 1 mm and 50 circular divisions, and a positive zero error of 0.02 mm. The main scale reads 4 mm and the 20th circular division coincides. Find the corrected reading.
questions.answer: The least count is 1/50 = 0.02 mm. The circular scale reading is 20 x 0.02 mm = 0.40 mm. The uncorrected reading is 4 + 0.40 = 4.40 mm. A positive zero error means the instrument reads more than the true value, so the correction must be subtracted. The corrected reading is 4.40 minus 0.02 = 4.38 mm.
questions.explanation: A positive zero error means the jaws close while the reading is still positive, so every reading is too large and must be reduced.
questions.commonMistake: Adding the positive zero error, which would give 4.42 mm instead of 4.38 mm.

questions.prompt: Why is it incorrect to use a spring balance to measure the weight of a body, and correct to say it measures the weight indirectly?
questions.answer: A spring balance works by comparing the force needed to stretch a calibrated spring with the force applied, and that comparison is valid only when the force is due to gravity. Pulling the spring sideways applies a force that stretches it without being a weight, so the reading would no longer correspond to gravity. The instrument therefore measures the magnitude of the gravitational force on the body, that is its weight, and does so by measuring the extension of the spring, so the weight is obtained indirectly.
questions.explanation: The balance is calibrated for vertical loading, so the reading is valid only for the gravitational force on the body.
questions.commonMistake: Claiming the spring balance measures mass directly, when the quantity read is a force and must be divided by g to obtain mass.

questions.prompt: Three measurements of the same length are 12.4 cm, 12.6 cm and 12.5 cm. If the instrument has a least count of 0.1 cm, what is the mean length and what is the greatest possible error in the mean?
questions.answer: The mean is (12.4 + 12.6 + 12.5)/3 = 37.5/3 = 12.5 cm exactly. Each individual reading carries an error of at most half the least count, that is 0.05 cm. Taking the mean of three such readings does not shrink the systematic part of the error, so the greatest possible error in the mean is still 0.05 cm. The true length is therefore between 12.45 cm and 12.55 cm.
questions.explanation: Averaging reduces random scatter between readings but cannot remove a systematic error, so the error of the mean stays at half a division.
questions.commonMistake: Dividing 0.05 cm by 3 as though averaging removed the uncertainty entirely, which is true only for purely random errors.

questions.prompt: A pendulum of length 0.81 m has a time period of 1.8 seconds. Find the value of g implied by these measurements, taking pi as 22/7, and comment on how it compares with the accepted value of 9.8 m per second squared.
questions.answer: Rearranging T = 2 pi root(l/g) gives g = 4 pi^2 l / T^2. Taking pi as 22/7, 4 pi^2 = 4 x (22/7)^2 = 4 x 484/49 = 1936/49 = 39.5102. So g = 39.5102 x 0.81 / (1.8)^2 = 32.0033 / 3.24 = 9.878 m per second squared. The accepted value is 9.8 m per second squared, so the experimental result is about 0.08 high, that is roughly 0.8 percent above the accepted value. This is a good result for a school experiment; the small excess is expected because the length is difficult to measure precisely, the stopwatch introduces a reaction-time error, and the bob is swung through a finite amplitude rather than an infinitesimal one.
questions.explanation: Rearranging the formula gives g = 4 pi squared times l divided by T squared. The result is close to the accepted 9.8 m per second squared, with the small excess explained by measurement and amplitude errors.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting to square the time period in the denominator, or leaving out the factor 4 in 4 pi squared, either of which changes the answer by a large factor.

questions.prompt: State the value of the acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface, and state two factors on which the weight of a body depends.
questions.answer: The acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface is 9.8 m per second squared, often rounded to 10 m per second squared. The weight of a body depends on the mass of the body, since W = mg, and on the strength of the gravitational field at the place, so the same body weighs less on the Moon than on the Earth.
questions.explanation: Weight is the product of mass and the local value of g, so it changes with place even though mass does not.
questions.commonMistake: Saying weight depends only on mass, forgetting that the value of g is not the same everywhere.
